data.title: Lichen striatus — viva
data.summary: Papulosquamous & erythroderma · 8 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Lichen striatus** (Papulosquamous & erythroderma)_

**Q1. What is lichen striatus?**
- Self-limited, acquired linear inflammatory dermatosis along Blaschko's lines, mainly in children 5–15 years (girls more)
- Thought to be a T-cell reaction to a trigger (viral infection, vaccine, trauma) against a mosaic clone of keratinocytes; associated with atopy

**Q2. Clinical features.**
- Sudden eruption of small (1–3 mm) pink, skin-coloured or hypopigmented flat-topped papules that coalesce into a continuous or interrupted band, usually unilateral on one limb (or trunk/neck), may be several centimetres long
- Usually asymptomatic or mild itch; nail involvement (longitudinal ridging, splitting, onycholysis) when the band reaches the finger
- Resolves in 6–12 months (up to 2 years) often leaving hypopigmentation (prominent in Indian skin)

**Q3. What are Blaschko's lines?**
- Lines of embryonic migration of epidermal (ectodermal) cells — V-shape on the back, S-shaped whorls on the abdomen, linear on limbs; they don't follow nerves, vessels or lymphatics; mark genetic mosaicism

**Q4. Differential diagnosis of linear lesions (PYQ: differential diagnosis for linear dermatoses).**
- Following Blaschko lines: lichen striatus, linear LP, ILVEN (inflammatory linear verrucous epidermal naevus — itchy, persistent, from early childhood, psoriasiform), epidermal naevus, linear psoriasis, linear porokeratosis, linear DLE/morphoea (en coup de sabre follows Blaschko), incontinentia pigmenti, blaschkitis (adult)
- Not Blaschko: Koebner lesions (LP, psoriasis, vitiligo), linear warts, zoster (dermatomal), sporotrichoid (lymphatic), phytophotodermatitis (streaks), dermatitis artefacta, linear scleroderma

**Q5. How to differentiate lichen striatus from ILVEN and linear LP.**
- Lichen striatus: sudden onset in a child, self-limiting in months, little itch, hypopigmentation
- ILVEN: onset in infancy, persistent, intensely itchy, psoriasiform/verrucous, resistant to therapy
- Linear LP: violaceous papules with Wickham's striae, adults, itchy, histology of LP, hyperpigmentation

**Q6. Histopathology.**
- Lichenoid/interface dermatitis with spongiosis and necrotic keratinocytes plus a deep perivascular and peri-eccrine/peri-follicular lymphocytic infiltrate — the peri-eccrine infiltrate is characteristic

**Q7. Treatment.**
- Reassurance — self-resolving
- Mild-to-moderate topical steroids or tacrolimus 0.03–0.1% for itch and to hasten resolution, emollients
- Post-inflammatory hypopigmentation recovers gradually; avoid aggressive treatment

**Q8. What is blaschkitis?**
- Adult counterpart with multiple linear bands along Blaschko's lines on the trunk, recurrent, more spongiotic histology — debated whether distinct from lichen striatus

## Quick spotter facts
- Child with sudden unilateral band of tiny flat papules on a limb along Blaschko's line — lichen striatus
- Peri-eccrine infiltrate on histology

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Lichenoid disorders; Linear dermatoses). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
